questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Solutions of an equation as a set
questions.learningObjective: explain how a solution set records the values that satisfy an equation
questions.stem: A note gives an equation in one variable and records the set of values of x that make it true.

answer.exemplar: The solution set of an equation is the set of values of the variable that satisfy it, written inside braces. For two x minus nine equals eleven, adding nine gives two x equals twenty and dividing by two gives x equal to ten, so the solution set is {10}. Listing solutions as a set matters because a set holds each member once, so the same value is never written twice, and the size of the set tells how many solutions there are.

questions.explanation: The solution set holds exactly the values of the variable that satisfy the equation, each written once. A linear equation in one variable has one such value.
questions.hint: Every member of the set must make the equation true.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Solutions of an inequality as a set
questions.learningObjective: explain how an inequality solution set is described
questions.stem: A note records an inequality and the set of values that satisfy it, and a translator wants to describe that set properly.

answer.exemplar: The solution set of an inequality is written in set builder notation, naming the variable and the condition it must meet, for example the set of all x with x greater than 2. The condition is kept in the same direction as the original inequality, since the set of values that satisfy an inequality is defined by that condition itself. Because an inequality on a variable over the reals has infinitely many members, a roster of a few values is only an abbreviation and never the whole set.

questions.explanation: The solution set names the variable and the condition it must satisfy, in the same direction as the original. Such a set has infinitely many members.
questions.hint: Name the variable and the condition it must meet.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Solution set of a compound condition
questions.learningObjective: explain how the joining word changes the size of a compound solution set
questions.stem: Two conditions joined together must be read for what the joining word means, because and and or give different counts.

answer.exemplar: A compound condition combines two sets, and the joining word decides how. With and, a value must satisfy both conditions, so the solution set is the intersection and its size is the overlap of the two sets. With or, a value satisfying either condition is enough, so the set is the union and its size is the two sizes less the overlap counted once. For example, the even numbers from 1 to 20 and the numbers above 10 meet both parts in five places, but they meet at least one part in fifteen.

questions.explanation: The word and asks for the intersection of the two sets, and the word or asks for the union. The counts differ because an overlap is counted once in a union.
questions.hint: Decide whether a value needs one part or both parts.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Whole numbers in a stated interval
questions.learningObjective: explain how to count whole numbers in an interval without listing them
questions.stem: A note asks for the whole numbers inside a stated interval, and the translator must count them without listing each one.

answer.exemplar: The whole numbers in a closed interval from a to b are counted by subtracting the lower end from the upper end and adding one, because the number of whole numbers from zero to n is n plus one. So from 10 to 20 inclusive the count is 20 minus 10 plus 1, that is eleven. The same rule handles an open end by adding one only when that end is included, and it always assumes the interval holds whole numbers rather than every real value.

questions.explanation: The count of whole numbers in a closed interval is the difference of the ends plus one, since counting from zero includes the zero. An open end changes it by one.
questions.hint: Count the steps between the ends and add one for the start.

questions.learningObjective: explain how to find every integer that meets a divisibility rule in an interval
questions.stem: A note asks for the integers in an interval that satisfy a divisibility rule, and the translator must include every qualifying value.

answer.exemplar: An integer is divisible by k when dividing it by k gives an integer quotient, so zero, the positive multiples of k and the negative multiples of k all satisfy the rule. In the interval from minus 12 to 12 the multiples of 5 are minus 10, minus 5, 0, 5 and 10, which is five values. Working from the lowest multiple at or below the lower end and stepping by the divisor finds them all, and checking that the last one is still within the interval counts them exactly.

questions.explanation: Zero and the negative multiples satisfy a divisibility rule just as the positive ones do. Working up from the first multiple at or below the lower end finds them all.
questions.hint: Start at the lowest multiple in the interval and step up.
